title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome due to nonadherence to antihypertensive treatment: A case report from Nepal
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of altered sensorium, bilateral upper-limb weakness, and slurred speech. She denied any seizure activity, tongue biting, or incontinence. Her medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin), hypertension (amlodipine and losartan), and primary hypothyroidism (levothyroxine), all of which she had taken for 10 years. She reported stopping her antihypertensive medications 1 week earlier. She did not smoke or drink alcohol, and her family history was noncontributory.

On examination her blood pressure was 210/110 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and Glasgow Coma Scale score 13/15. Her random blood glucose was 140 mg/dL. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic examination revealed motor strength of 3/5 in the left upper limb and 5/5 in the right upper limb; 5/5 in the left lower limb and 4/5 in the right lower limb. No visual field deficits were noted. Fundoscopic examination showed grade 1 hypertensive retinopathy.

Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, triglycerides 430.7 mg/dL, TSH 9.7 IU/mL, and HbA1c 9.31%. Echocardiography revealed grade 1 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction. An immediate noncontrast head CT scan was normal, and a CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism. Despite the normal initial CT, ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis remained considerations.

On hospital day 2, a repeat noncontrast CT scan of the head demonstrated bilateral symmetrical white matter hypodensities in the frontal lobes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial broad differential including stroke, transient ischemic attack, encephalitis, and cerebral venous thrombosis was made — “In our patient, we considered differentials such as stroke, transient ischemic attack, encephalitis, and cerebral venous thrombosis.”  
2. Ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis were deemed less likely after a normal head CT — “Since her head CT scan was normal, ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis were less likely. However, ischemic stroke was still a possibility due to early CT imaging.”  
3. Encephalitis was excluded by cerebrospinal fluid analysis — “During her ICU stay, we did a lumbar puncture, which was normal, and ruled out encephalitis.”  
4. Seizure disorder was excluded by electroencephalography — “Also, her electroencephalogram (EEG) was not suggestive of seizure disorder.”  
5. A provisional diagnosis of hypertensive encephalopathy was made based on clinical and radiographic findings — “Based on the detailed evaluation, we diagnosed the patient with hypertensive encephalopathy.”  
6. The reversibility of white matter lesions on follow-up imaging supported the diagnosis of PRES — “On follow-up after 2 weeks, a head CT scan was normal. This pointed towards the diagnosis of PRES.”
